item.title: What’s left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days
item.description:
The diplomatic battles shaping the future of climate action

• Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun).

But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.

item.title: Pakistan cruise to eight-wicket win over Sri Lanka to seal Test series 1-0
item.description:
Pakistan wrapped up an eight-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the second and final Test, chasing down a target of 90 in just 13 overs to seal the two-match series 1-0 on Friday.

The hosts needed only 90 minutes on the fourth morning to complete the job after Mohammad Abbas dismissed the last Sri Lankan batter to end the visitors’ second innings at 316.

It was Pakistan’s first Test win since they beat the West Indies in the summer and their first series victory in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle.

The result was also just their third win in 11 matches in the current cycle, following draws against South Africa and the West Indies and series defeats in Bangladesh and England.

The first Test against Sri Lanka, also played in Rawalpindi, had ended in a draw.

Sri Lanka, who had resumed at 309-9, added seven runs before Asitha Fernando was trapped lbw for two by Abbas. Fernando reviewed the decision, but ball-tracking showed the delivery clipping the top of middle stump.

Abbas finished with three wickets for 55 runs from 34 overs, including 15 maidens. Aamer Jamal also claimed three wickets for 67, while Razaullah took two for 116 and Saqib Khan one before being sidelined by a hamstring injury.

Sri Lanka’s total left Pakistan needing 90 for victory, with Milan Rathnayaka unbeaten on 66 from 88 balls, including 12 fours.

His fighting innings had been central to a recovery after the visitors were dismissed for 98 in their first innings and conceded a 227-run lead when Pakistan replied with 325.

Pakistan’s pace attack had made full use of a green-tinged pitch to bowl Sri Lanka out cheaply on the opening day and put the hosts firmly in control.

The tourists began their second innings 153 runs behind and slipped to 10-2, but half-centuries from Kusal Mendis (53), Sonal Dinusha (54) and Rathnayaka helped them reach 316 and avoid an innings defeat.

Their 235-run effort on the third day briefly revived the contest, although the eventual target remained modest.

Pakistan began the chase positively, with Azan Awais and Tayyab Arif putting on 18 for the opening wicket. The stand ended when Lahiru Kumara bowled Tayyab for 13, with the batter beaten by movement off the pitch after striking three fours.

Azan was joined by Mohammad Taha, but the latter’s stay was brief. Asitha Fernando trapped him lbw for four, and Taha’s review failed as the ball was shown to be clipping leg stump. Pakistan were 37-2, but Sri Lanka could not build on the breakthrough.

Aamer was promoted up the order and turned the chase into a brisk finish. He struck 34 not out from 22 balls, hitting five fours and a six, and added an unbroken 53 with Azan for the third wicket.

Aamer attacked from the outset, taking boundaries off Fernando and Kumara before finishing the match with a four off Prabath Jayasuriya. Azan remained unbeaten on 32 from 36 balls, with five fours, as Pakistan reached 90-2 in 13 overs.

item.title: 10,000 constable, 4,000 SI posts approved: How will the recruitment process work?
item.description:
All administrative hurdles to large-scale recruitment in the Bangladesh Police have been cleared as the government has finalised the approval to recruit 10,000 constables and 4,000 sub-inspectors (SIs) directly.

There are now no remaining obstacles to recruiting a total of 14,000 personnel.

All official procedures, including approval from the Ministry of Public Administration, the Ministry of Finance and the Secretaries Committee, have already been completed.

As a result, the Bangladesh Police can formally begin the recruitment process at any time.

The final approval has created a major opportunity for those who have been preparing to join the police force for a long time. Notably, this is the first time all 4,000 SI posts are being filled through direct recruitment.

The Police Regulations of Bengal (PRB) have been amended for this purpose. Previously, 50 per cent of SI posts were filled through departmental promotions and the remaining 50 per cent through direct recruitment.

Besides, the government is also considering holding a special Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination to recruit 400 to 500 officers to the post of assistant superintendent of police (ASP)

Current status of the recruitment process

Asked about the latest developments and administrative preparations for the large-scale police recruitment, Tanvir-Al-Nasif, deputy secretary at the Ministry of Home Affairs, told Prothom Alo on Thursday that there were no longer any obstacles to starting the recruitment process.

He said all administrative procedures for recruiting 10,000 constables and 4,000 SIs had been completed, including approval from the Ministry of Public Administration, the Ministry of Finance and the Secretaries Committee. The Bangladesh Police can now begin the recruitment process at any time.

Meanwhile, Kamarum Munira, assistant inspector general (Media and Public Relations) at Police Headquarters, provided details about the ongoing constable recruitment circular. She told Prothom Alo that a total of 102,694 jobseekers from across the country had applied online under the ongoing circular.

Explaining the recruitment plan, Kamarum Munira further said there were currently 2,000 vacant constable posts in the police force. In addition, approval had been granted to recruit 10,000 new constables.

Considering the recruitment process, the plan is to fill the existing 2,000 vacancies along with another 4,000 posts from the newly approved 10,000 through the ongoing recruitment circular. This means a total of 6,000 constables are likely to be recruited through the current process. The remaining 6,000 newly approved constable posts will be filled gradually through subsequent recruitment circulars.

Earlier, a recruitment circular for constables across the country was published on 9 October. Although applications closed on 30 October, the circular did not specify the number of posts. However, if the number of posts increases to 6,000, competition among candidates will be considerably lower than in the previous recruitment drive.

In the recruitment circular issued in April, 126,000 applications were submitted against 2,703 posts. At the time, 47 candidates were supposed to compete for each post. With the increase in the number of posts this time, an average of only 17 candidates will compete for each position.

How the recruitment selection process works

Candidates for constable and SI posts in the police force are selected through a rigorous screening process. For constable posts, candidates must pass preliminary screening, physical measurement, physical endurance tests, a written examination and a psychological test.

Recruitment for SI posts, on the other hand, is completed in several stages. Initially, applicants undergo physical measurement and document verification. They must then pass running and physical fitness tests. In the next stage, candidates sit for a written examination and a computer proficiency test. Finally, the Police Headquarters selects candidates through intelligence and viva voce tests.

For both positions, candidates will be screened based on merit and qualifications as well as intelligence reports. If an applicant provides false information in the application or at any stage of the selection process, their candidature will be cancelled immediately.

An SI serves as a highly important field-level officer in the police administration. Maintaining general diaries (GDs) at police stations and investigating criminal cases are among their primary responsibilities. They also work directly in the field to prevent crime, collect intelligence, arrest suspects and maintain overall law and order in their respective areas.

Grades and benefits of SI and constable posts

Sub-inspectors (SIs) and constables are two important positions in maintaining law and order at the field level in the country.

According to the national pay scale, an SI is a Grade 10 government employee. The starting basic salary for the position is Tk 32,000, rising to a maximum of Tk 77,300.

On the other hand, a trainee recruit constable (TRC) falls under Grade 17. After completing training and receiving permanent appointment, a constable receives a starting basic salary of Tk 9,000, rising to a maximum of Tk 21,800.

In addition to their basic salaries, both SIs and constables receive several allowances and benefits under government regulations. These include house rent allowance depending on the area of posting, medical allowance, risk allowance, festival allowance, and tiffin and travel allowances.

They are also provided with uniforms free of cost at government expense, subsidised ration facilities for themselves and their families, and advanced medical services. During training, they also receive prescribed allowances and accommodation facilities.

Based on merit and qualifications, employees in both positions have opportunities for promotion to higher ranks in the future.

Denmark ratifies security deal with US and Greenland
item.description:
Denmark’s parliament on Thursday ratified a security agreement with the US over Greenland, hoping to end tensions after US President Donald Trump had repeatedly demanded control over the autonomous Danish territory.
In the Danish 179-seat parliament, all 109 members present voted in favor of the text. Greenland’s parliament already ratified the deal in early November.
US ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the ratification, saying in a post on X: “The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of Nato.”
The trilateral security and military access agreement between Washington, Nuuk and Copenhagen allows for expanded US military presence on the mineral-rich and strategically located island in the northern Atlantic.
It also includes permission to establish a “Golden ‌Dome” ​missile defense system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
The island is home to some 57,000 people and is strategically located along the shortest route from Europe to North America. It already is home to the northernmost US military base.
The deal was signed in September by Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen but still needed ratification from lawmakers in Greenland and Denmark.
In January 2026, Trump renewed calls for Greenland to become part of the US, threatening military action and tariffs against European allies if they opposed him.
He argued that Denmark was not able to protect the autonomous Arctic territory from threats by China and Russia. His demands strained US relations with Denmark and alarmed European Nato allies.
Tensions somewhat eased in late January when Trump and Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte announced a “concept of a deal” that would expand US military access to Greenland. This then led to the agreement being signed in September.
Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has broad military access to Greenland. Denmark had repeatedly said it was open to expanding the US military presence on the island but rejected Trump’s demand for full US control.

item.title: Riyadh skyscraper damaged as Saudi reports new Houthi attacks
item.description:
A skyscraper in Riyadh housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund was damaged on Thursday, witnesses told AFP, as the kingdom reported new attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited over the summer in neighboring Yemen’s civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
In the early hours of Thursday, AFP journalists in the Saudi capital reported a powerful blast had been heard.
Around the same time, civil defense authorities issued a warning for “potential danger” but said minutes later that the danger had passed.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had “addressed a missile threat launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh”.
“Initial assessment indicates the impact of debris, with material damage currently being surveyed,” said coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki.
Witnesses later told AFP that Riyadh’s Public Investment Fund Tower, which at 80 stories is the tallest in the city’s financial district, had been damaged.
“The facade is damaged across several floors, with windows blown out,” said one source who requested anonymity. Two other sources confirmed the damage.
Standing 385 meters high, the tower dominates King Abdullah Financial District, which acts as a showcase for Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions.
With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.
Chaired by Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the sovereign wealth fund is one of the largest in the world with more than $900 billion in assets under management.
It is also one of the main instruments for diversifying the kingdom’s economy away from oil, plans which have been threatened by the latest fighting.
Malki also said Thursday that the coalition had intercepted five ballistic missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia’s southern region, which borders Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking targets including airports, energy infrastructure, military sites and Riyadh’s financial district.
In October, a deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds, forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks.
In response, the Saudi coalition has been striking Houthi targets in areas of Yemen held by the group.
On Thursday, Houthi media outlets reported that Saudi Arabia had launched another attack on Yemen’s capital Sanaa.
The Almasirah television channel said Saudi forces have “once again targeted the shoe and textile factory of the Alyateem Development Foundation,” citing its correspondent in Sanaa.
The Saudi coalition said it had “destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Dhamar,” a city about 100 kilometers (60 miles) south of Sanaa that was used by the Houthis to strike Riyadh.
The long-running civil war in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, fell dormant in 2022 after a ceasefire was implemented, but sprang back to life this summer.
The Houthis are now nearing Aden, the internationally recognized government’s interim capital, having made sweeping territorial gains since the war resumed.
More than 1,600 people have been killed in the latest round of fighting and more than 300,000 displaced, according to the United Nations.
On Thursday, the Saudi crown prince met with US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh, according to state news agency SPA.
The two sides “reviewed bilateral relations, particularly in the military fields, and discussed regional developments”, the media outlet said.
On Wednesday, another powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh, with residents saying no mobile phone alerts were issued beforehand, as is usually the case.
“The explosion was extremely loud,” said one resident in the north of the city. “Hearing a blast without receiving a warning is very frightening.”
The coalition said it had intercepted two drones launched by the Houthis in the Riyadh and southern regions.
The military spokesman for the Houthis, Yahya Saree, said in a post on X that the group had targeted Riyadh’s international airport and the capital’s financial district with cruise missiles.

item.title: Special exit facility for settling NPLs, BB issues fresh instructions to banks
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank (BB) has instructed banks to make use of the ‘special exit’ facility to expedite the recovery of non-performing loans (NPLs).

Under the facility, borrowers may settle their loans through a one-off payment, with both charged and uncharged interest waived subject to certain conditions. Each such settlement, however, must be approved by the board of directors of the respective bank.

The central bank disclosed this in a circular issued today, Thursday. The directive has been sent to the managing directors and chief executive officers of all scheduled banks in the country.

Bangladesh Bank said it had issued the Policy on Special Exit for Recovery or Adjustment of Non-performing Loans on 29 June to recover defaulted loans in the banking sector.  The latest instructions have been issued to ensure proper implementation of the policy and accelerate loan recovery.

The new instructions come amid a substantial volume of defaulted loans in the banking sector. At the end of September, the amount of defaulted loans in the country’s banking sector stood at Tk 597,154.93 crore, accounting for 32.17 per cent of total outstanding loans. 

Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury disclosed the figures in parliament on 16 November.

What is the special exit facility?

The special exit facility is a mechanism through which a defaulting borrower can negotiate with a bank to settle outstanding loan liabilities by making a one-off payment, subject to specified conditions. 

Under this arrangement, banks may waive interest on loans. However, borrowers must pay the agreed settlement amount in a single instalment to discharge their liabilities.

Bangladesh Bank introduced the special exit facility through a policy circular issued on 29 June. On the same day, Prothom Alo carried a report on it. The report said borrowers with bad or loss-category classified loans would be allowed to settle their liabilities by repaying the principal in a single payment. The previous stringent conditions for waiving charged and uncharged interest on bank loans were also relaxed. The initiative was primarily aimed at reducing banks’ unrecovered loans and enhancing their capacity to extend fresh credit.

Under Bangladesh Bank’s policy, loans classified as bad or loss-category as at the cut-off date of 30 June 2026 will be eligible for the special exit facility. The facility may be granted on the basis of the banker-customer relationship, subject to approval by the bank’s board of directors.

The policy also relaxed certain existing conditions for waiving charged and uncharged interest. Previously, banks were required to ensure recovery of their cost of funds before granting an interest waiver. This requirement has been relaxed under the special exit facility.

As a result, both state-owned and private commercial banks will be able to offer borrowers the opportunity to settle their loans through one-off payments after waiving interest, subject to the prescribed conditions. However, the facility is not automatically available to all defaulting borrowers.

Who is eligible for the facility?

According to Bangladesh Bank’s policy issued on 29 June, loans classified as bad or loss-category on 30 June 2026 will be eligible for the special exit facility. Loans classified as bad or loss-category that were rescheduled between 6 August 2024 and 30 June 2026 may also be considered for the facility.

The central bank has instructed banks to give priority to short-term agricultural loans and loans to cottage, micro and small industries when extending the special exit facility. Thus, alongside eligible large borrowers, small entrepreneurs and borrowers in the agricultural sector will also be able to benefit from the arrangement.

item.title: Chase confirms cyberattack that may have exposed customer data. Here’s what we know
item.description:
Chase Bank isn’t doing much to reassure customers.

The bank said Thursday that third-party vendors were recently targeted in a cyberattack that resulted in a breach of some customer information. But there is “no connection” between this cyber attack and the outage earlier this week that saw customers unable to log in to their accounts, the bank posted on X.

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” Chase said in the post, without specifying when the breach occurred.

JPMorgan Chase, parent company of the bank, was one of several financial institutions to experience outages on Monday that saw many customers unable to log in to their accounts for several hours. A string of high-profile outages in the past week has upended work and air travel, while keeping Americans locked out of various websites. Even a highly classified network for internal communications at the National Security Agency also experienced an outage.

Another day, another data breach shouldn’t surprise most Americans at this point. But paranoia has been proliferating online about a more coordinated takedown of our tech infrastructure—and even though Chase said the cyberattack and outage are unrelated, some people aren’t buying what the largest U.S. bank is saying.

The New York-based company previously blamed the disruptions on Monday on a “software bug” that was resolved and said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or a systemic issue. 

So to announce a cyberattack a few days later has only raised more questions. A spokesperson for JPMorganChase didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from Fast Company.

Cybernews reported Thursday that the ransomware gang n0n dumped on the dark web the stolen data of some 16,000 JPMorganChase customers and employees on Thursday after a 48-hour ransom had passed. The hackers said it had allegedly stolen information related to Chase’s premium Reserve credit card program that’s marketed to affluent Americans, as the outlet reported.

The most popular comment on a subreddit discussing that news report came from a Redditor who posted: “We are being lied to by the government.” That sort of refrain has become increasingly common as people have become more paranoid that something more nefarious is happening. 

RUBIO TRIES TO REASSURE

As conspiracy theories have flourished online in the wake of these outages, that’s led some Americans to panic-buying items at Costco, as Bloomberg reported. Meanwhile, a petition on Change.org to “demand full transparency” about these recent tech disruptions has yet to garner much support.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has seemingly taken on the task in the Trump administration of trying to calm the nerves of Americans. Speaking on Tuesday during a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump, Rubio said the government has “no evidence” of a link between the outages or that they’re the result of cyberattacks, as Politico reported. 

“We fully acknowledge that this is unsettling to see these reports day after day of some technical failures,” Rubio told reporters on Tuesday. “We have no evidence, no indications of any kind that these incidents are related to each other or that any of them have anything to do with a malign actor, with a cyber criminal.”

Washington Should Allow Ukraine to Hit Russia's Ballistic Missile Launchers
item.description:
Earlier this month I traveled to Ukraine and met with soldiers, corps commanders, and business leaders in Kyiv, Dnipro, Pavlohrad, and Kharkiv. I was in Kyiv on November 7 when Russia launched 36 ballistic missiles overnight toward the capital and the region around it. Ukrainian air defenses stopped four. The attack was aimed mainly at energy infrastructure, three days before negotiators met in Abu Dhabi.

I want to make the case for allowing Ukraine to hit the launchers that fire these missiles. What Ukraine needs is a White House approval, not a new weapon: permission to use Starshield, SpaceX's satellite service for military customers, as far as 300 kilometers into Russia and only against ballistic missile launchers. This is good for the United States. It would put pressure on Russia to negotiate seriously, there is no cost to us, and it is not complex.

The problem

Russia strikes Kyiv and Dnipro with its own Iskander ballistic missiles and with North Korean KN-23s. It fires them from mobile launchers spread across four regions: Voronezh, Kursk, Oryol, and Bryansk. Ukrainian officers put the number of launchers at about 65. A launcher typically stays at its firing position for only a few minutes before it relocates.

Ukraine does not have enough interceptors to stop these missiles. President Zelensky said on October 27 that Ukraine has received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States this year.

Ukraine began going after the launchers in May. Its officers describe the results so far as limited: some launchers damaged, few destroyed. They say Ukraine can now locate the launchers in most cases. What it cannot do is get a large enough warhead to them before they move. The drones Ukraine sends that far into Russia are controlled through radio relays and carry small payloads, so a hit usually damages a launcher without destroying it. Ukraine's bigger drones, with payloads of up to about 200 kilograms, fly on a Starshield link, which Ukraine has over occupied territory but not inside Russia.

If Starshield were available to Ukraine across a strip of Russian territory extending roughly 300 kilometers from the border, the officers believe they could destroy the majority of the launchers in it or force Russia to pull them back. In their judgment, Russia's ground-launched ballistic missiles would then no longer reach Kyiv, Dnipro, or the power plants of central Ukraine. Kharkiv would probably remain within range, and missiles launched from aircraft would not be affected. I cannot verify this estimate, but it comes from officers who have spent six months trying to hit these launchers.

Why this is good for the United States

Ukraine's army is holding the front, and the commanders I met expect to keep holding it. Russia has not been able to break through on the battlefield, so it is putting pressure on Ukraine's civilians instead. During my visit, some households in Kyiv without a generator were down to two hours of electricity per day. Russia is terrorizing civilians to pressure Ukraine's government, and ballistic missiles are the part of that campaign Ukraine has the hardest time stopping. On November 7, Ukraine stopped 149 of 172 drones but only four of 36 ballistic missiles.

The Kyiv Independent reported on November 18 that the Kremlin believes it has the advantage in the talks. It pointed to two factors: Russia's strikes on Ukraine's energy system continue, and Ukraine is struggling to get enough interceptors. It also said the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi showed little interest in an energy ceasefire. The talks produced an agreement in principle on a prisoner exchange, but no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory.

If Ukraine can destroy the launchers or push them out of range, Russia loses much of its ability to hit Kyiv and Dnipro with ballistic missiles. That removes much of the pressure on civilians that Russia is counting on. Without it, Russia has less reason to believe it can win by waiting and more reason to negotiate seriously. I cannot say for certain that Russia would then agree to a settlement, but it has little reason to compromise while these attacks are working. Some have argued that allowing these strikes would not help end the war. I think the opposite is true.

Every launcher destroyed also means fewer missiles to intercept, at a time when we are short of interceptors ourselves. CSIS estimates that the war with Iran used up about half of our Patriot interceptors.

What it would take from Washington

There is no cost to the United States. Ukraine builds the drones and flies them, so no American weapons, interceptors, or new funding are needed.

It is also not complex. Ukraine already uses Starshield on its strike drones over occupied Ukraine, and the service ends at the Russian border. Ukraine reports that a speed limit has interfered with those flights this month; SpaceX says it has imposed none. The service is already controlled by terminal and by location, so letting registered Ukrainian terminals work 300 kilometers into Russia is a change to settings that have been changed before.

The decision belongs to the White House. Elon Musk has said that the U.S. government owns and controls Starshield, and that the U.S. military and ultimately the president decide the limits on its use.

The approval can be narrow: ballistic missile launchers only. This autumn, Washington objected to Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, and refineries would not be covered. Ukrainian officers say each terminal is registered individually, and that inside this strip they would move their strikes away from economic targets and onto military ones.

The White House should make this decision now. Ukrainian officers say Russia already protects some of its fixed sites with satellite jamming and is likely to have mobile jammers in a few months. Approving it would help protect civilians in Kyiv and Dnipro this winter, at no cost to the United States, and would give Russia a real reason to negotiate.

item.title: Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president?
item.description:
Will Saddam Haftar be Libya’s next president? Expert comment thilton.drupal 20 November 2026

The son of commander Khalifa Haftar has consolidated his position as heir apparent and expanded his influence. But his pursuit of the presidency could bring Libya back into conflict.

Saddam Haftar, the son of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF) commander Khalifa Haftar, has recently visited several foreign capitals in an apparent attempt to boost his international standing. This has been seen as part of a concerted push to become Libya’s next president.

This effort will define Libya’s politics for the coming months. It has huge implications for the country’s political future amid a US-led push for a national government that would unify Libya’s two rival administrations: the LAAF-controlled administration in eastern Libya and the Government of National Unity (GNU) in Tripoli. Strong opposition to Saddam’s goals in western Libya also means that the risk of conflict is increasing.

Saddam becomes heir apparent

For many years, there have been questions over Khalifa Haftar’s succession. The assumption has been that Haftar, 83, would remain in direct control of the LAAF while alive. It was speculated that the LAAF could fragment without Haftar, given the LAAF’s status as a hybrid of a military institution and a family enterprise.  

However, in recent years, Haftar has increasingly taken a back seat as his sons Saddam, Khaled, Belgassim and al-Sadiq have come to the fore. Their rise became clearer after the failure of the LAAF to capture Tripoli in 2020, which led Haftar to reassess his approach. Over subsequent years, the LAAF was restructured. Its forces were placed under the command of Saddam and Khaled, who gained responsibility for land forces and security units respectively. 

Meanwhile, Belgassim developed strong networks and influence in political circles. He was instrumental in the formation of a new government that sought to replace the sitting GNU in Tripoli. In 2023, Belgassim also assumed the helm of the Libyan Development and Reconstruction Programme, formed after floods killed several thousand people in Derna, which provided a new narrative of development for the Haftar family.

However, Khalifa’s appointment of Saddam as deputy general commander in August 2025 sealed his position as heir apparent. Saddam has become the most powerful of the sons through not just his military position, but also his alleged increasing influence via proxies over the oil and gas and banking sectors in eastern Libya.

The Boulos initiative

Saddam’s rise is important in the context of the push for a unified government in Libya. This has been led by Massad Boulos, the US Special Advisor for Africa and the Middle East. Under Boulos’ plan, a unified government would be formed as part of a deal between the two ruling families: the Haftars, who control eastern Libya, and the Dabaibas, who control the Tripoli-based GNU.

While the US has not publicized the parameters of the deal, insiders have said that Saddam Haftar would become a member of the Presidency Council, the three-person body whose chairman is Libya’s de facto head of state. The Dabaiba family would retain the prime minister’s post.

Related work

Why US plans for power-sharing in Libya will not work

Negotiating processes had previously focused on seeking agreement between Libya’s fractious institutions: the chronically divided House of Representatives in eastern Libya and the Tripoli-based High State Council. But the US plan has broken with this formula, instead seeking agreement between the Haftars and the Dabaibas. The first agreement made through this channel was a deal on budgetary spending in April 2026.

Subsequently, the United Nations adapted to the new format. The UN Mission’s ‘4+4’ committee brought together a combination of representatives from the GNU, LAAF, the House of Representatives and the High State Council. The 4+4 reached agreement on a roadmap for national elections in August.

This pivot towards negotiations being between the LAAF and the GNU – essentially between the emissaries of Saddam Haftar and the Dabaibas – is more significant than the content of the agreement. It officially places Saddam’s LAAF General Command as a negotiating party with parity with the internationally recognized GNU.  

Path to the presidency?

Buoyed by these diplomatic advances, Saddam has recently made significant moves to expand his influence.

The ousting of the longtime speaker of the House of Representatives in October – and his replacement with a figure known for his support for the LAAF – is widely understood to have been orchestrated by Saddam.

Shortly after, the House of Representatives moved to ratify a controversial memorandum of understanding with Turkey over the recognition of drilling rights in the eastern Mediterranean. Insiders have said privately that Saddam pushed for this move, which angered Egypt and European countries, presumably with the aim of securing Ankara’s support for his push for the presidency in return.

Then, on 26 October, the governor of the Central Bank of Libya was replaced, reportedly due to a private agreement between the Haftars and the Dabaibas. The Central Bank holds a critical place in the management of Libya’s economy, overseeing the distribution of foreign currency and dinar payments that are so crucial to Libya’s leaders.

That same week, Saddam was in Turkey for talks with the GNU on military reunification.

Alongside strengthening his influence over important institutions in Libya, Saddam has consequently emerged as the apparent partner of preference for the some of the most influential international actors. He is seen as someone who can get things done and maintain order in comparison to the messy picture of contested power in western Libya.

The enduring Haftar ‘problem’ and the risk of conflict

Saddam is now central to any political effort to reunify the country. His ambitions to enter Tripoli are widely known. Those familiar with the security sector in the capital note that local allies of Saddam are seeking to prepare the ground for his arrival.

But opposition to – and mistrust of – Saddam in western Libya remains strong, especially in key constituencies such as the city of Misrata. This has not been helped by the uncovering of a sleeper cell, allegedly linked to the LAAF, that was accused of seeking to cause damage to oil and gas infrastructure in the city of Zawiya in August.

Many doubt that Saddam is willing to share power. It therefore seems no meaningful guarantees can be provided to Saddam’s opponents to reassure them. Western Libyan actors would like to separate the discussion of military reunification from political reunification as a result.

Consequently, while the Dabaiba family may be willing to cut deals to retain a modus vivendi with Saddam, it is highly unlikely to sign a deal making Saddam president. This is evident in the fact that no deal has yet been reached, despite intensive efforts over months by Boulos.

This, in turn, creates a problem. It is not clear how Saddam’s rapid rise and apparent aspirations for president can be squared with his opponents’ steadfast opposition to him. And they are unlikely to go anywhere, considering that the Dabaibas are entrenched in power too.

This fundamental difference runs deeper than the Boulos initiative. As one source in the security sector told me: even if there were elections, Saddam would not accept the results if he loses, and his opponents would not accept the results if he wins.

If Saddam continues to push for the presidency, Libya therefore faces a heightened risk of conflict. Many of his opponents would seemingly prefer the messy situation in Tripoli to prevail over a new order that could ultimately end up squarely under Saddam’s control. But, given the strength of international support building behind Saddam’s campaign, their options are narrowing.

item.title: The ICJ’s Myanmar finding shifts the dial – a little – on the grounds for a guilty verdict in a genocide case
item.description:
The ICJ’s Myanmar finding shifts the dial – a little – on the grounds for a guilty verdict in a genocide case Expert comment jon.wallace 20 November 2026

The Court’s unusually split decision seems to adjust how intent to destroy a group ‘in whole or in part’ is established.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the highest court in the world, has ruled that Myanmar is guilty of genocide. According to the Court, the ‘clearance’ campaign by the Myanmar military against its Rohingya minority of 2017 was aimed at the destruction, in whole or in part, of that community. The finding in this case, which was brought before the Court by the Gambia in 2019, will reverberate far beyond Myanmar and its immediate environment.

The ICJ’s previous genocide cases

The Rohingya are a mainly Muslim ethnic group that has been excluded from Myanmar citizenship and discriminated against for decades. In the wake of attacks by terrorist groups against the military in 2016, some 10,000 Rohingya were killed, and over 85 per cent of its population of around 850,000 were displaced from Myanmar over the following year in a campaign of killings, rape and the burning of villages.

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

The ICJ has established a very high bar for confirming that genocide has occurred. Several cases, including those brought by Croatia against Serbia and Sudan against the UAE, have been unsuccessful. 

Others are still ongoing, addressing the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, Ukraine and the Russian Federation, and Gaza.

Only once before, in relation to the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of 8,000 men and boys in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has the ICJ confirmed genocide. But controversially, it failed to attribute the atrocity to its alleged author, the Republic of Serbia (then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia) under Slobodan Milosevic.

This new decision of the Court moves the dial ever so slightly, reducing the legal hurdles on the way towards a finding of genocide. 

The grounds for a finding of genocide

According to the Genocide Convention of 1948, genocide requires three elements. 

First, it must be directed against a protected group, defined by national, ethnic, racial or religious characteristics. Second, there must be prohibited acts directed against members of the group. This includes killings, causing serious bodily or mental harm, inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of the group, or measures intended to prevent births or forcibly transferring children to another group. 

But critically, even if a pattern of such practices is clearly evident, this must be carried by the specific intent to destroy the group as such ‘in whole or in part’ – the third element.

This may seem odd. If the result is the destruction of the group, one might argue that this should suffice to constitute genocide. Such conduct would clearly amount to a crime against humanity and other severe violations of human rights and humanitarian law. However, in defining what is sometimes called ‘the crime of crimes,’ the Genocide Convention imposes this additional criterion of specific intent. 

Of course, that is difficult to prove. States no longer record their decision to commit genocide in a formal document, as Hitler’s government did in the famous 1942 Wannsee Protocol, which planned the complete destruction of Europe’s Jewish population. 

Without such formal documentation, proof of the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part must be inferred from the nature of a systematic campaign of killing and other acts proscribed by the Genocide Convention that are directed at a defined population segment.

Previously, the Court asserted that such an inference can only be made if this pattern cannot be explained by any reason other than the intention to commit genocide. 

In its defence, Myanmar offered several alternative grounds to explain the nature of its armed campaign. It referred to the need to mount a counter-terrorism effort following attacks by rebel movements in Rakhine province, where most Rohingya used to reside. However, in view of the Court, this motivation would not explain the pattern of brutal attacks against the civilian population.

The Court also considered whether Myanmar’s conduct might simply have been directed at the forcible displacement of the Rohingya, rather than their destruction in whole or in part. This alone would be a serious international crime, but it would not quite amount to genocide.

However, the Court looked at the overall context of the long-standing campaign against the Rohingya – including discrimination, hate speech, the nature of the military operation and other culpable acts systematically targeting this group and affecting its ‘foundations’ or existence.

In broadening this overall context, and relying on the totality of the evidence, rather than just the well attested reports of individual atrocities, the Court was able to assert that the intent to commit genocide was the only reasonable inference that could be drawn.

The effect on other cases

This outcome will concern some governments involved in other ongoing cases regarding genocide. 

Ukraine brought a case before the ICJ in 2022, asking the Court to confirm that it had not committed genocide against Russian-speakers on its territory – a central claim made by Russia to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that year. 

In another case, the DRC is alleging that Rwanda is involved in genocide conducted on its territory. In a further action, Nicaragua is alleging that Germany shares responsibility for the alleged genocide in Gaza due to its supply of arms to Israel. 

The Court’s Myanmar judgement may impact these cases. But international attention is mainly focused on the case’s implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. 

In an initial, provisional phase of the case, the Court found that there may be a plausible case of genocide in relation to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

Counsel for Israel and South Africa, along with the over 20 others states that have intervened in that case, will now assess the Court’s finding and ask: what would the outcome be if the matrix of factors applied by the ICJ in the Myanmar case were applied to Israel’s armed campaign in Gaza? Would this exercise demonstrate that the intent to commit genocide is the only reasonable explanation for the character of that campaign?

Related work

South Africa’s genocide case against Israel: The International Court of Justice explained

The key clauses in the Myanmar judgement were adopted by an unusually divided Court, by a majority of 9 to 6. The ICJ decides according to the applicable law, not the politics involved in a given situation. But its decision will probably be criticized by some as having lowered the threshold for the identification of genocide, perhaps with a view to confirming the relevance of the Court and of the international rule of law. International law has been largely disregarded in many recent conflicts – especially its humanitarian provisions. 

On the other hand, those opposing the Court’s finding might be accused of trying to prevent a precedent being established when it comes to evaluating the Gaza case.

In addition to political controversy, the case raises another important issue: A third state, The Gambia – which is not involved in Myanmar’s conflict – managed to obtain a ruling in favour of a dispossessed and internationally disenfranchised minority group located a continent away. 

The Gambia brought the action with the support of the Organization of the Islamic Conference and senior international lawyers, adopting a kind of international public service role in defence of the international public order. It confirmed that all states have a firm legal interest in compliance with that rule by all other states, and that parties to the Genocide Convention can bring a case to the Court in defence of the prohibition of genocide. 

The Court even considered that in this case between The Gambia and Myanmar, it has the authority to rule on the entitlement of the Rohingya as the ultimate beneficiaries of the obligation to prevent genocide to restitution and compensation from their own government. In this way, it has reasserted and indeed extended its role of guardian of the international rule of law at a time of challenge to global order.

Symbolically, the meeting was unprecedented, but in substance it produced modest results: Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping, and Donald Trump talked for an hour and a half and adopted a declaration that touches on several important issues but sticks to general language. Commentators concluded that the summit was no repeat of the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States divided postwar Europe into spheres of influence. Meduza has gathered what outlets in the United States, Europe, Ukraine, Russia, and China are saying about the summit.

item.title: Gold price cut by Tk12,815 per bhori
item.description:
Gold and silver prices have fallen again in the domestic market, with the price of 22-carat gold dropping by Tk12,815 per bhori to Tk201,109.
The new rates came into effect at 10am on Friday.
The Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) announced the revised prices following a meeting of its Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring on Friday morning.
In a statement, the association said the prices were revised in consideration of the overall market situation following a decline in the prices of pure gold and silver in the local market.
Under the new rates, 22-carat gold is priced at Tk17,245 per gram, or Tk201,109 per bhori (11.664 grams).
The price of 21-carat gold has been set at Tk16,470 per gram, or Tk192,349 per bhori, while 18-carat gold will cost Tk14,145 per gram, or Tk164,866 per bhori.
Gold under the traditional method has been priced at Tk11,560 per gram, or Tk134,859 per bhori.
On Thursday (November 19), 22-carat gold was priced at Tk213,924 per bhori, meaning the latest revision represents a reduction of Tk12,815.
Silver prices have also been reduced.
Under the new rates, 22-carat silver will cost Tk260 per gram, or Tk3,003 per bhori.
The price of 21-carat silver has been set at Tk250 per gram, or Tk2,916 per bhori, while 18-carat silver will cost Tk215 per gram, or Tk2,508 per bhori.
Silver under the traditional method has been priced at Tk165 per gram, or Tk1,925 per bhori.
Previously, 22-carat silver was priced at Tk290 per gram, 21-carat at Tk275, 18-carat at Tk235 and traditional silver at Tk180 per gram.
Bajus said the prescribed selling prices of gold and silver jewellery already include VAT, meaning jewellers cannot charge buyers VAT separately. However, making charges will apply depending on the design and type of jewellery.
For exchanges of old gold jewellery, a 12% deduction will apply to the prescribed price after excluding making charges and the cost of stones. For purchases of old gold jewellery, the deduction will be 18%.
No additional VAT deduction is allowed in either case, the association said.
The revised prices will remain effective at all jewellery establishments across the country until further notice, Bajus added.

item.title: Humaiun: Dhaka eyes Rohingya repatriation within 18 months
item.description:
Bangladesh will step up talks with the United Nations and bilateral partners to secure safe passage for Rohingyas back to Myanmar within 12 to 18 months, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said.
"We will pursue these discussions vigorously so that we can provide safe passage within a year to a year and a half," he told journalists at a media briefing on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) judgment on Rohingya genocide.
Kobir said the ruling gave Bangladesh a stronger legal basis to press for safe repatriation and compensation for affected communities.
He outlined the timeframe in response to a question on how Bangladesh would accelerate repatriation, saying that any return would depend on putting safeguards in place in Myanmar's Rakhine State so that the Rohingyas could go home safely and rebuild their lives.
The state minister said Bangladesh would work with UN agencies, key regional partners and other stakeholders to establish conditions for safe return.
In his prepared remarks, he described prompt and sustainable repatriation as the only effective solution to the protracted crisis.
Kobir said Bangladesh would also work through the UN system and with its bilateral partners to ensure that compensation is provided to affected Rohingya communities.
Asked whether Dhaka would pursue a bilateral mechanism with Myanmar to determine compensation, he said bilateral efforts alone could not secure the necessary reparations and that the process would require the involvement of several countries and agencies.
He said financial compensation could never make up for the lives lost or the suffering of bereaved families.
Bangladesh would, however, he said, seek to persuade Myanmar to provide compensation and take other measures that would help surviving family members return and rebuild their lives.
Kobir said Bangladesh would work within the UN system to press for follow-up on compensation if The Gambia, a party to the case, brought the matter before the UN Security Council.
Asked whether Bangladesh would formally propose deploying an international peacekeeping force in Rakhine, Kobir said Dhaka would engage a wider range of UN agencies and bilateral partners if the matter came before the council. He gave no commitment to a formal peacekeeping proposal.
He said that the ICJ had found Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine State.
The state minister described it as the first judgment in the court's history to find a state responsible for committing genocide.
He said the court recognised the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group with their own language, culture and identity, and noted that discriminatory laws, restrictions and campaigns of hatred had progressively curtailed their rights over several decades.
Kobir said the court found that Myanmar had failed to prevent genocidal acts by individuals acting alongside its security forces and to preserve evidence as required by its 2020 order on provisional measures.
He said the court directed Myanmar to enact effective legislation to prevent genocide, end ongoing violence and investigate individuals reasonably suspected of involvement in genocide, with prosecution and punishment where appropriate.
The ruling also addressed reparations for victims through restitution and compensation, he added.
Kobir said the judgment was final, could not be appealed and was legally binding on the parties to the case.
Bangladesh, which hosts around 1.3 million forcibly displaced Rohingyas, had closely followed the proceedings although it was not a party to the case, he said.
The state minister thanked the government and people of The Gambia for bringing the case on Nov 11, 2019, as well as the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and the 11 countries that filed written declarations before the court.
He also acknowledged the Rohingya community's years of advocacy and the support of host communities in Cox's Bazar.
Kobir urged the international community to act swiftly on the judgment and called on development partners and donors to continue humanitarian assistance for displaced Rohingyas and Bangladeshi host communities until repatriation is complete.
Foreign Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury was present at the briefing, among others.

item.title: Xi-Trump-Putin summit: What did it achieve?
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world’s three most powerful military powers amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
Xi hailed the talks as “groundbreaking,” saying discussions ranged from global governance and denuclearization to the war in Ukraine and energy security.
The “peace declaration” released after their meeting made no mention of Russia’s war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.
Instead, the three leaders agreed to pursue reforms of the United Nations, limit the role of the International Criminal Court and reaffirm their commitment to avoiding nuclear war. They also pledged to boost supplies of refined petroleum products to address global energy challenges.
The tightly choreographed meeting fueled concerns that Beijing, Washington and Moscow could seek to reshape the international order around competing spheres of influence.
While Xi said the talks with Trump and Putin were “positive, constructive and fruitful,” Trump heralded the gathering as “really making history.”
For Putin, the three-way talks, and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier, offered a chance to show the world that he was on par with the leaders of the US and China, despite Western efforts to isolate him since he launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Emma Chanlett-Avery, senior director for Political-Security Affairs at the Asia Society Policy Institute (Aspi), said Putin had the most to gain from the meeting as “he appeared on the world stage as one of the dominant players in the world.”
Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), echoed this view.
The meeting itself is a “major outcome for Russia,” he told DW, pointing to Russian media coverage that has cast it as “reinforcing Russia’s standing in the world.”
The joint statement also said the leaders are committed to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February.
Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.
But Beijing has so far been reluctant to accept limits as its estimated arsenal of around 500 warheads remains far smaller than those of Russia and the US.
Moscow and Washington are believed to possess more than 5,000 warheads each.
Lee said China is unlikely to participate in a trilateral institutionalized setting to control nuclear arms.
“The gap between China’s nuclear arsenal and those of Russia and US is still quite large. From China’s perspective, it doesn’t seem to make a lot of sense to put the three powers in the same bucket in this area.”
The expert believes Trump attended the meeting as he is “actively thinking about his legacy in the final two years in office.”
“So, in this context, the idea of setting up a trilateral nuclear arms control arrangement would have been a very big achievement,” Lee said.
But, in the end, the declaration said the countries would merely engage in “dialogue” on the issue, avoiding any explicit commitments to downsize their nuclear stockpiles.
China initially hesitated to organize the trilateral summit as it did not want to be explicitly tied to Russia’s war in Ukraine and harm Beijing’s efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
The Chinese government, which is working to rebalance economic ties with the EU, was also wary of appearing to form a G3 club with Washington and Moscow, which could alienate other global partners.
Chanlett-Avery said that China had some degree of discomfort in convening this meeting, worried about getting involved in Ukraine issues.
But Beijing eventually “managed to get the outcome they wanted” and kept the European conflict out of the meeting’s focus, she noted.
“China was able to show off Shenzhen and all of its sparkling high-tech features. They convened a successful international meeting that grabbed lots of headlines,” she added. “So, I think China probably came out feeling okay.”
Prior to the summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a “second Yalta,” referring to the Yalta Conference held in Crimea in 1945.
That meeting saw the Allied powers decide on the post-war European order following the end of World War II.
In Shenzhen, Putin stressed that Russia, the US and China, as victors in World War II and veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council, bore a “joint responsibility for maintaining international peace.”
But Ying-Yu Lin, Associate Professor at Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Taiwan’s Tamkang University, said the Yalta comparison “is a bit of a stretch,” given the vast differences between 1945 and now.
Putin also said that all three leaders “agree that it’s a useful format,” and such meetings could take place again.
Lee, the EIU expert, said the trilateral setup “is unlikely to be just a one-off” and there will probably be more such meetings in the coming years.
“Especially from the US side to have this kind of setup, there will be some interest in maintaining warm relations with both China and Russia,” he underlined.

item.title: Secret AL contact: 300 plus police under investigation
item.description:
Who is speaking to the exiled leaders of the banned Awami League, from where, and through which apps and phones?
Intelligence agencies are now working to find out exactly that, following several incidents in quick succession that exposed covert communications between police officers and the banned party’s leaders.
The revelations have sparked fear among police personnel considered close to the party.
Police Headquarters sources say internal investigations are under way against more than 300 police personnel over allegations of maintaining secret contact with Awami League leaders and activists. The list includes officers ranging from sub-inspectors (SIs) to deputy inspectors general (DIGs).
Police Super Jahangir Alam of the Chittagong Range Reserve Force has already been caught. Earlier, Rakibul Hasan, former officer-in-charge (OC) of Dhaka Cantonment Police Station, was arrested in a sedition case.
The names of Awami League leaders have also surfaced in connection with crude bomb blasts, arson and vandalism in several parts of the country.
As a result, questions have emerged among the public over whether the police are taking action against everyone involved. Intelligence agencies are now focusing on covert activities within the police force.
Asked about the issue, Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed told Dhaka Tribune on Tuesday night that there was no specific information on how many police personnel considered close to the Awami League had been identified. However, he said the police were working professionally to prevent sabotage.
The commissioner said the administration and law enforcement agencies were taking special measures on the ground to prevent sabotage and disorder.
“Some 177 checkpoints have been set up across Dhaka, and many of our members, from senior officers to office-based personnel, are now deployed in the field. Personnel at the checkpoints are equipped with body cameras. Around 400 Honda patrol vehicles are operating round the clock across all police stations, alongside mobile patrols. The DB and SRU are also conducting mobile patrols. Besides the DB, other intelligence agencies are working as well.”
He said the situation was being monitored using drones. CCTV cameras had also been installed at key points across Dhaka and along the elevated expressways, with the installation work still underway, as several recent cocktail attacks involved explosives being thrown from flyovers.
Mosleh Uddin said the police were prepared to deal with any situation.
“Ordinary people are also helping us by providing information. Over the past 25 days, 50 people involved in sabotage have been arrested. The police are bringing those involved in sabotage and terrorist activities to justice to prevent fear among the public. If any police officer is found to be involved, strict action will be taken,” he said.
Md Shafiqul Islam, additional commissioner and head of the DMP Detective Branch (DB), also spoke to Dhaka Tribune on Tuesday. He said Awami League leaders and activists involved in arson and terrorist activities had been arrested.
Detectives are working in the field to prevent sabotage, while mobile patrols, Honda patrol vehicles and CCTV cameras have been deployed at various locations, he said.
He added that between September and November 17, a total of 1,229 people had been arrested on allegations of involvement with the Awami League or in criminal activities, including sabotage.
Asked about the number of police personnel aligned with the Awami League who were on the blacklist, he said lists had been prepared previously and were still being updated, but the number was nowhere near 22,000. Investigations were under way to establish who was involved.
“If any police member helps bring the Awami League back to the country, strict action will be taken against them,” he said.
A section of government officials has become a source of concern for the government. Many officials who benefited politically in terms of recruitment, postings and promotions during the Awami League government, whose activities are now banned, continue to hold key administrative positions.
Allegations against them include maintaining contact with Awami League activists, leaking information and using political influence to retain advantageous positions under the current government.
Home ministry sources say the government has placed more than 300 administrative officials, from field administration offices to the Secretariat, under surveillance. Preparations are also under way for a major reshuffle in the field administration, with changes expected in 25 deputy commissioner (DC) posts.
The government fears that a section of administration cadre officials close to the Awami League remains active. Questions have resurfaced over the roles of some officials in field administration and law enforcement agencies. Some are allegedly leaking important government information, while others are helping leaders and activists of the banned Awami League in various ways.
A section of the government's policymakers believes that failure to identify politically influenced officials within the administration could create problems in maintaining law and order, gathering intelligence and implementing government decisions. The Gopalganj incident has brought these concerns further to the fore.
Following the incident, Gopalganj DC Md Arif-uz-Zaman was withdrawn and Superintendent of Police Md Habibullah was transferred. Chuadanga DC Lutfun Nahar was also attached to the Ministry of Public Administration.
Md Abdul Bari, state minister in charge of the Ministry of Public Administration, said: “I am receiving daily intelligence reports on the activities of each of the administration's 800,000 officials and employees. The DCs of two districts have already been withdrawn, and investigations into them are ongoing. Social media activities are also being verified. If such allegations are established against any official, action will be taken. The current government is taking a stricter stance on these matters.”
The Home Ministry has said that following the July mass uprising, 147 officers of the rank of assistant superintendent of police (ASP) and above were sent into compulsory retirement in the public interest. In addition, departmental cases were filed against 62 officers of the BCS police cadre on charges of abandoning their posts after August 5, 2024.
Of the 62 officers, 31 have been dismissed from service, while departmental proceedings against the remaining 31 are ongoing.
The information was presented recently at the fifth meeting of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Home Affairs at the National Parliament.
Several senior Police Headquarters officials said investigations were under way against more than 300 police personnel, with action being taken against those found to have links to the Awami League.
The meeting also discussed measures to restore police morale. MP Abdul Baten said that the July mass uprising had not only caused damage to police infrastructure and vehicles but had also severely affected the morale and mental well-being of police personnel. He asked whether special training programmes and a separate budget allocation were in place to restore their morale.
Manjur Morshed Chowdhury, senior secretary of the Home Ministry, said regular training programmes were being conducted to boost police morale. He added that police personnel had faced various obstacles and hardships in performing their duties in the aftermath of the uprising, particularly due to mob violence.
The home secretary also said immediate legal and administrative action would be taken against those responsible for attacking police officers at police stations.
Dr Tawohidul Haque, a Dhaka University teacher and crime expert, told Dhaka Tribune on Tuesday night that if police personnel aligned with the Awami League were placed on a blacklist, it would emerge that they had all been recruited under different governments.
“So, if we remove them, we will have to remove everyone,” he said.
He said that once a person became a servant of the Republic, their duty was to serve the country and its people, not to publicly display a political identity. However, many officials appeared comfortable declaring their political affiliations and enjoying various benefits in the name of a party.
“Our system is responsible for this. We must come out of this system,” he said.
The crime expert said the police should not belong to any political party and that the force should be restructured accordingly.
Those who commit crimes must be identified and held accountable, he said, warning that removing personnel wholesale would weaken the police force and leave it unable to even make effective use of its existing strength.
That, he added, made the current situation particularly concerning.

item.title: Amir Khosru: Govt plans to turn Chittagong into economic, logistics hub
item.description:
The government plans to transform Chittagong into an economic and logistics hub for the entire country, going beyond its traditional role as the commercial capital, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury has said.
“Under the prime minister’s special interest and full support, initiatives have been taken to expand Chittagong Port’s capacity, build deep-sea ports, upgrade Chittagong Airport to international standards, and develop cargo villages and cold-chain facilities. The development of Chittagong means the development of the entire country,” he said.
He made the remarks while addressing the inaugural ceremony of the 32nd International Trade Fair, organised by the Chittagong Chamber of Commerce and Industry at the Railway Polo Ground in the port city on Friday afternoon.
The minister said the government planned to unlock the economic potential of all regions by establishing deep-sea ports in several locations, including Maheshkhali, and energy hubs centred on Chittagong and Khulna.
He said the Asian Development Bank (ADB) was providing financing for infrastructure expansion, including the development of Chittagong Airport and the logistics sector.
Under the ADB Framework Agreement, a nationwide development programme worth around $80 billion has been undertaken through the Integrated Growth Network Development (IGND) project, with most of the investment earmarked for Chittagong, he added.
Amir Khosru said plans to address electricity and gas shortages had been finalised, with significant progress expected in the energy sector over the next two years.
“Once these development plans are implemented, Bangladesh will become a trillion-dollar economy by 2034,” he said.
He stressed that economic development was not solely the government's responsibility, urging business leaders, politicians and people from all walks of life to work together.
He said the benefits of development must reach every citizen through the democratisation of the economy, increased investment and employment generation.
Special guest Chittagong City Corporation Administrator Dr Shahadat Hossain said acts of arson and violence were taking place in different parts of the country, but the authorities would ensure Chittagong remained safe.
He said around Tk2,500 crore had been spent on development projects in the city over the past two years to make it more business-friendly.
A cycle track has also been developed as part of efforts to make Chittagong more tourist-friendly, he added.
The guests formally inaugurated the fair by cutting a ribbon and releasing balloons.
The month-long international trade fair will remain open daily from 10am to 10pm at the Railway Polo Ground.

Govt to rebuild Bangladesh as fascism-free dignified state: PM
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Saturday, said his government is committed to rebuilding a fascism-free Bangladesh as a dignified and exemplary state on the world stage, pledging continued respect and support for freedom fighters and their families.

"The government's pledge is to place the independent Bangladesh, which the valiant freedom fighters courageously established for us, in a position of dignity," he said, adding that the state would continue to extend respect and support to the freedom fighters and their families to the best of its capacity and resources.

The Prime Minister was addressing a reception for gallantry award-winning freedom fighters of the Armed Forces and their heirs on the occasion of Armed Forces Day-2026. The reception was held this morning at the Army Multipurpose Complex in Dhaka Cantonment.

Noting that freedom fighters were conferred gallantry titles such as Bir Sreshtha, Bir Uttam, Bir Bikram and Bir Protik for their heroic role in the Liberation War, the Prime Minister said more important than any title is the glory of fighting for and winning a nation's independence.

"Not everyone gets the opportunity to achieve such glory in a lifetime. That is why the freedom fighters are unique and extraordinary," he said.

Addressing the freedom fighters and family members present, he said some of them had the good fortune to take part directly in the Liberation War, while others lost family members as martyrs. "All of you share that glory, directly or indirectly. I extend my heartfelt congratulations to you," he said.

Recalling the sacrifices of 1971, the Prime Minister said independent Bangladesh was established at the cost of the lives of millions, the honour of countless mothers and sisters, and the sacrifices of those who were wounded and crippled.

He paid deep respect to all martyrs of the Liberation War, expressed profound sympathy and condolences to the wounded freedom fighters and the families of martyrs, and prayed for the salvation of the departed souls.

Describing felicitation of the freedom fighters as a responsibility of the state, he said the honour and reception accorded to them on the historic Armed Forces Day reflect the state's obligation to them. "By honouring them, the state has tried, at least to some extent, to discharge that obligation," he said.

Identifying himself as the son of a freedom fighter, Tarique Rahman said he was proud to attend the programme, and that any glory or success of the Liberation War and the freedom fighters moves him deeply. He said Major Ziaur Rahman, the proclaimer of Bangladesh's independence, was himself a proud member of the armed forces, which was also a matter of pride for the force.

The Prime Minister said that every time the BNP has been given the responsibility of running the state by the people's mandate, it has taken various positive steps for the Liberation War and the welfare of freedom fighters.

He said the late former prime minister Khaleda Zia established the Ministry of Liberation War Affairs in 2001 to uphold the glory of the Liberation War and ensure the welfare of freedom fighters, a decision that later proved timely. The Jatiya Muktijoddha Council Act was enacted in 2002, he added.

Highlighting the freedom fighters' contribution, he said many of them are now weary with age, but the glow of independence still shines in their eyes in the twilight of their lives.

He thanked all concerned for the commendable initiative the Armed Forces Division takes every year to formally honour these 'living legends' scattered across the country.

The Prime Minister concluded his speech by paying deep respect once again to the martyrs of the Liberation War.

Earlier, the premier paid homage to the martyred members of the Armed Forces by placing a wreath at the altar of Shikha Anirban in Dhaka Cantonment. After laying the wreath, he stood in solemn silence for a while as a mark of profound respect for the martyrs.

A contingent of the Army, Navy and Air Force presented a guard of honour while the bugle sounded the last post. The prime minister later signed the visitors' book kept at the memorial.

On arrival at Shikha Anirban, the Prime Minister was received by his Defence Adviser Brigadier General (Retd) Dr AKM Shamsul Islam, Army Chief General Waqar-Uz-Zaman, Navy Chief Admiral Khondkar Misbah Ul Azim, Air Chief Air Chief Marshal Hasan Mahmood Khan and Principal Staff Officer of the Armed Forces Division Lieutenant General Mir Mushfiqur Rahman.
